[1] write a simple z.prop.test()
```{r}
z.prop.test <- function(p1, n1, p2 = NULL, n2 = NULL, p0, 
                          alternative = "two.sided", c.level = 0.95) {

  # p1 stands for proportion of sample 1
  # n1 stands for sample 1 size
  # p2 is set to null if not specificy and it will. perform one sample z test, if specify it stands for proportion for sample 2
  # n2 is same logic as above and if specifiy it stands for  sample 2 size
  # p0 stands for true population proportion in one sample test
  # alternative is set to two sided and the alternative hypothesis would be p1 is different from 01, if set to less than it would be testing if p1 < p0, if set to greater than if would be testing p1 > p0
  # CI stands for confidence interval, which by default is set to 95%
  
  if (is.null(p2) || is.null(n2)) {
    # if there is no input for p2 and n2 we will proceed with a one sample z test
    if (n1 * p0 <= 5 || n1 * (1 - p0) <= 5) {
      warning("Warning: Assumption for Normal Distribution Might Not be Valid.")
    }
      # this is to ensure the validity of assumping normal distribution
    
    se_null <- sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n1) # calculat standard error for proportion under null hypothesis
    
    Z <- (p1 - p0) / se_null # calculate the Z statistic which is useful later for calculating p value
    
       # Calculate p value based on input into "alternative"
    if (alternative == "two.sided") {
      # For a two-sided test
      p_value <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(Z))
    } else if (alternative == "less") {
      # For a 'less than' test: H1: p1 < p0, we use the lower tail.
      p_value <- pnorm(Z)
    } else if (alternative == "greater") {
      # For a 'greater than' test: H1: p1 > p0,  we use the upper tail.
      p_value <- pnorm(Z, lower.tail = FALSE)
    } 
    
    # calculate sample standard error for making the CI, note here we are using 1-p1, for the se_null we were using 1-p0
    se <- sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1) / n1)
    
    # find the Z(alpha/2)
    z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - (1 - c.level) / 2)
    
    # Make the upper and lower bound confidence interval for p1
    CI <- c(p1 - z_alpha * se, p1 + z_alpha * se)
    
    # Return the results as a list.
    return(list(Z = Z, P = p_value, CI = CI))
    
  } else {
    # the following is for processing the two sample test; if p2 and n2 is specify, we are testing for the difference between two proportion, the null hypothesis here is H0: p1 - p2 = 0
    
    # Check the validity of normal distribution assumption for both sample
    if (n1 * p1 <= 5 || n1 * (1 - p1) <= 5) {
      warning("Warning: Assumption for Normal Distribution Might Not be Valid.")
    }
    if (n2 * p2 <= 5 || n2 * (1 - p2) <= 5) {
      warning("Warning: Assumption for Normal Distribution Might Not be Valid.")
    }
    
    # Calculate the standard error for the difference in proportions.
    se_diff <- sqrt((p1 * (1 - p1) / n1) + (p2 * (1 - p2) / n2))
    
    # Compute the Z statistic. notice the formula is different for two sample test 
    Z <- (p1 - p2) / se_diff
    
    # Calculate p value based on input into "alternative"
    if (alternative == "two.sided") {
      p_value <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(Z))
    } else if (alternative == "less") {
      # For 'less', we test if p1 is significantly less than p2.
      p_value <- pnorm(Z)
    } else if (alternative == "greater") {
      # For 'greater', we test if p1 is significantly greater than p2.
      p_value <- 1 - pnorm(Z)
    }
    
    # creating CI for the difference in proportions
    z_alpha <- qnorm(1 - (1 - c.level) / 2)
    CI <- c((p1 - p2) - z_alpha * se_diff, (p1 - p2) + z_alpha * se_diff)
    
    return(list(Z = Z, P = p_value, CI = CI))
  }
}

```

[2] Fit a simple linear regression model to predict longevity (MaxLongevity_m) measured in months from species’ brain size (Brain_Size_Species_Mean) measured in grams.
```{r}
library(curl) # load the curl library
library(ggplot2)

# inspect the kamilar and cooper data
f <- curl("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/fuzzyatelin/fuzzyatelin.github.io/master/AN588_Fall23/KamilarAndCooperData.csv")
a <- read.csv(f, header = TRUE, sep = ",", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# there are a lot of NAs to be removed
d <- subset(a, !is.na(Brain_Size_Species_Mean) & !is.na(MaxLongevity_m))

#creating the normal model using lm
model1 <- lm(MaxLongevity_m ~ Brain_Size_Species_Mean, data = d)

 

# extracting the coefficient for the normal regression line
coef_model1 <- coef(model1)
intercept <- round(coef_model1[1], 2) # this takes the intercept value from th  coefficients we just extracted
slope <- round(coef_model1[2], 2) # this takes the value at the second position which is the slope
eq_label <- paste0("y = ", intercept, " + ", slope, " * x")

#next we can create the scatter plot with the normal regression line
p1 <- ggplot(d, aes(x = Brain_Size_Species_Mean, y = MaxLongevity_m)) +
  geom_point() +  # Plot the data points
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "blue") +  #  
  geom_text(x = max(d$Brain_Size_Species_Mean)*0.5, 
            y = max(d$MaxLongevity_m)*0.5, 
            label = eq_label, 
            color = "red", size = 5, hjust = 0) +
  labs(x = "Brain Size (g)", y = "Max Longevity (months)",
       title = "Longevity vs. Brain Size with Fitted Regression Line")

p1

confint(model1, level = 0.90)

###response: from the summary we can see that the slope estimate is 1.218 and it means that for every addtional grams in brain size, the model predicts that the maximum longevitiy increase by about 1.218 monts on average.since the p value for the point estimate of the slope is  < 2e-16 which is extremely small, we reject the null hypothesis and there is strong evidence that brain size is a statically significant predictor of longevity; the 90% confidence interval for Brain_Size_Species_Mean is approximately (1.0356, 1.4004) meaning that we are 90% confident that the true increase of longevitiy is between 1.036 abd 1.400 months with one additional grams.

# Create a new data frame spanning the range of Brain_Size_Species_Mean
new_data <- data.frame(Brain_Size_Species_Mean = seq(min(d$Brain_Size_Species_Mean, na.rm = TRUE), 
                                                     max(d$Brain_Size_Species_Mean, na.rm = TRUE), 
                                                     length.out = 100))

# Get predictions with 90% confidence intervals
pred_conf <- predict(model1, newdata = new_data, interval = "confidence", level = 0.90)
# Get predictions with 90% prediction intervals
pred_pred <- predict(model1, newdata = new_data, interval = "prediction", level = 0.90)

# Combine predictions with new_data
new_data$fit      <- pred_conf[, "fit"]
new_data$lwr_conf <- pred_conf[, "lwr"]
new_data$upr_conf <- pred_conf[, "upr"]
new_data$lwr_pred <- pred_pred[, "lwr"]
new_data$upr_pred <- pred_pred[, "upr"]

# Create the plot with original points, the fitted line, and the interval bands
p2 <- ggplot(d, aes(x = Brain_Size_Species_Mean, y = MaxLongevity_m)) +
  geom_point() +  # Original data points
  # Fitted regression line from our model
  geom_line(data = new_data, aes(x = Brain_Size_Species_Mean, y = fit, color = "Fitted"), size = 1) +
  # 90% Confidence interval lines (upper and lower)
  geom_line(data = new_data, aes(x = Brain_Size_Species_Mean, y = lwr_conf, color = "90% Confidence"), 
            linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
  geom_line(data = new_data, aes(x = Brain_Size_Species_Mean, y = upr_conf, color = "90% Confidence"), 
            linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
  # 90% Prediction interval lines (upper and lower)
  geom_line(data = new_data, aes(x = Brain_Size_Species_Mean, y = lwr_pred, color = "90% Prediction"), 
            linetype = "dotted", size = 1) +
  geom_line(data = new_data, aes(x = Brain_Size_Species_Mean, y = upr_pred, color = "90% Prediction"), 
            linetype = "dotted", size = 1) +
  labs(x = "Brain Size (g)", 
       y = "Max Longevity (months)",
       title = "Longevity vs. Brain Size with Fitted Regression,\n90% Confidence and Prediction Intervals",
       color = "Legend") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Fitted" = "blue", 
                                "90% Confidence" = "pink", 
                                "90% Prediction" = "purple")) +
  theme_minimal()


p2



# Create a new data frame for a brain weight of 800 gm
prediction_point <- data.frame(Brain_Size_Species_Mean = 800)

# Generate the prediction with a 90% prediction interval
prediction_800 <- predict(model1, newdata = prediction_point, interval = "prediction", level = 0.90)
prediction_800

#response: the point estimate for the maximum longevitiy is about 1223.345 months and there is a 90 confidence that the actual max longevitiy is between 1021 and 1424. I dont really trust the model prediction since in our model, the max brain size was around 500 gram and 800 grams is way outside of the observed rnage and extrapolation betound the data can be unreliable.
```

```{r}
# Fit the log-transformed model
model2 <- lm(log(MaxLongevity_m) ~ log(Brain_Size_Species_Mean), data = d)

# Extract coefficients and create the regression equation label
coef_model2 <- coef(model2)
intercept_log <- round(coef_model2[1], 2)  # intercept on the log scale
slope_log <- round(coef_model2[2], 2)      # slope on the log scale
eq_label_log <- paste0("log(y) = ", intercept_log, " + ", slope_log, " * log(x)")

# Create the scatterplot with the log-transformed data and fitted regression line
p1_log <- ggplot(d, aes(x = log(Brain_Size_Species_Mean), y = log(MaxLongevity_m))) +
  geom_point() +  # Plot the log-transformed data points
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "blue") +  # Fitted regression line
  geom_text(x = max(log(d$Brain_Size_Species_Mean), na.rm = TRUE)*0.5, 
            y = max(log(d$MaxLongevity_m), na.rm = TRUE)*0.5, 
            label = eq_label_log, 
            color = "red", size = 5, hjust = 0) +
  labs(x = "log(Brain Size (g))", y = "log(Max Longevity (months))",
       title = "Log-Log: Longevity vs. Brain Size with Fitted Regression Line")

p1_log

# Display the 90% confidence interval for the slope parameter
confint(model2, level = 0.90)

###response: from the summary we can see that the slope estimate is 0.234 and it means that a 1% increase in brain size is associated with an approximate 0.23415% increase in maximum longevity. the p value is really small and we reject the null hypothesis and there is sufficient evidence to suggest that brain size is a statistically significant predictor of longevity in this model. The confidence interval is between 0.2 and 0.26 meaning that we are 90 percent confident that the true increase in maximum longevitiy for each addtional gram is between 0.2% and 0.26%.


# Create a new data frame spanning the range of Brain_Size_Species_Mean
new_data_log <- data.frame(Brain_Size_Species_Mean = seq(min(d$Brain_Size_Species_Mean, na.rm = TRUE), 
                                                         max(d$Brain_Size_Species_Mean, na.rm = TRUE), 
                                                         length.out = 100))

# Get predictions (in log scale) with 90% confidence intervals
pred_conf_log <- predict(model2, newdata = new_data_log, interval = "confidence", level = 0.90)
# Get predictions (in log scale) with 90% prediction intervals
pred_pred_log <- predict(model2, newdata = new_data_log, interval = "prediction", level = 0.90)

# Combine predictions with new_data_log
new_data_log$fit      <- pred_conf_log[, "fit"]
new_data_log$lwr_conf <- pred_conf_log[, "lwr"]
new_data_log$upr_conf <- pred_conf_log[, "upr"]
new_data_log$lwr_pred <- pred_pred_log[, "lwr"]
new_data_log$upr_pred <- pred_pred_log[, "upr"]

# Create the plot with the interval bands on the log-log scale
p2_log <- ggplot(d, aes(x = log(Brain_Size_Species_Mean), y = log(MaxLongevity_m))) +
  geom_point() +  # Original data points (log-transformed)
  # Fitted regression line (from the predictions)
  geom_line(data = new_data_log, aes(x = log(Brain_Size_Species_Mean), y = fit, color = "Fitted"), size = 1) +
  # 90% Confidence interval lines (upper and lower bounds)
  geom_line(data = new_data_log, aes(x = log(Brain_Size_Species_Mean), y = lwr_conf, color = "90% Confidence"), 
            linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
  geom_line(data = new_data_log, aes(x = log(Brain_Size_Species_Mean), y = upr_conf, color = "90% Confidence"), 
            linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
  # 90% Prediction interval lines (upper and lower bounds)
  geom_line(data = new_data_log, aes(x = log(Brain_Size_Species_Mean), y = lwr_pred, color = "90% Prediction"), 
            linetype = "dotted", size = 1) +
  geom_line(data = new_data_log, aes(x = log(Brain_Size_Species_Mean), y = upr_pred, color = "90% Prediction"), 
            linetype = "dotted", size = 1) +
  labs(x = "log(Brain Size (g))", 
       y = "log(Max Longevity (months))",
       title = "Log: Longevity vs. Brain Size with Fitted Regression,\n90% Confidence and Prediction Intervals",
       color = "Legend") +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Fitted" = "blue", 
                                "90% Confidence" = "pink", 
                                "90% Prediction" = "purple")) +
  theme_minimal()

p2_log

# Create a new data frame for a brain weight of 800 gm
prediction_point_log <- data.frame(Brain_Size_Species_Mean = 800)

# Generate the prediction with a 90% prediction interval (results are on the log scale)
prediction_800_log <- predict(model2, newdata = prediction_point_log, interval = "prediction", level = 0.90)
prediction_800_log

#response: while even in the log transformed model we are still doing extrapolation, I am more confident that the normal model since the 90% confidence range is much smaller. I think the log transformed model is a more sutiable model for explaning the relationship between brain size and longevitiy.
```
